text: For carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae producing NDM (metallo-beta-lactamase), the first choice is ceftazidime-avibactam combined with aztreonam, after a synergy test shows a zone of inhibition.
caveat: Ceftazidime-avibactam alone is inactive against NDM; here avibactam protects aztreonam, so use the two together only after a synergy test.

text: Other option for NDM (metallo-beta-lactamase) K. pneumoniae: a polymyxin plus another agent with demonstrated susceptibility, such as tigecycline, an aminoglycoside or IV fosfomycin, or a carbapenem when its MIC is low. Avoid polymyxin B for UTI.
caveat: NDM defeats carbapenems; a carbapenem is listed only as a polymyxin partner when the measured carbapenem MIC is low.

text: For mild CRAB infection a single active agent may suffice; sulbactam, for example as ampicillin-sulbactam, is the agent of choice, even when non-susceptibility is reported.
For moderate to severe CRAB infection, combine at least two active agents, always including sulbactam, for example with a polymyxin, minocycline or tigecycline.
Polymyxins are a treatment option for CRAB; use colistin rather than polymyxin B for urinary infection.
Minocycline is a treatment option for CRAB infection.
Tigecycline is a treatment option for CRAB infection but should not be used for urinary tract infection.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or an aminoglycoside can be used for CRAB if the isolate is susceptible.
For carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa, use ceftazidime, cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam when in-vitro susceptibility is demonstrated.
Aminoglycosides are an option for carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa when in-vitro susceptibility is demonstrated.
Polymyxins are reserved for carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa infections with no other treatment option.
For severe CRPA infection susceptible only to polymyxins, aminoglycosides or fosfomycin, a polymyxin-based combination with another agent the isolate is susceptible to is suggested.

Cefiderocol is a Reserve antibiotic whose primary use is targeted treatment of severe infection by metallo-beta-lactamase-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales such as NDM-producing K. pneumoniae.
Cefiderocol is reserved for targeted treatment of laboratory-confirmed carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, particularly metallo-beta-lactamase producers such as NDM-producing E. coli.
Cefiderocol can be used for severe laboratory-confirmed carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa infection, particularly with metallo-beta-lactamase producers such as VIM.
Ceftazidime-avibactam is reserved for severe laboratory-confirmed carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales infection; it is active against KPC producers.
Ceftazidime-avibactam is reserved for severe laboratory-confirmed carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales infection; it is active against OXA-48 producers.
Ceftazidime-avibactam is inactive against NDM, VIM and IMP metallo-beta-lactamases unless it is given together with aztreonam.
caveat: Ceftazidime-avibactam alone is inactive against NDM; it is useful only given together with aztreonam, which avibactam protects.

text: Ceftazidime-avibactam is reserved for severe laboratory-confirmed carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa infection susceptible to it; it is not for A. baumannii.
IV fosfomycin is reserved for severe carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales infection susceptible to it, usually in combination because resistance emerges quickly when used alone.
IV fosfomycin is salvage therapy for otherwise untreatable MRSA infections susceptible to it.
Linezolid is used for MRSA infection in selected situations: severe renal impairment, vancomycin hypersensitivity, or a need for oral treatment when cheaper oral options are unsuitable.
Meropenem-vaborbactam is reserved for severe laboratory-confirmed KPC-producing Enterobacterales infection, including isolates resistant to ceftazidime-avibactam but susceptible to it.
Meropenem-vaborbactam is a Reserve option for KPC-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales such as E. coli; it is not active against metallo-beta-lactamase or OXA-48 producers.
Plazomicin is reserved for severe carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales infection susceptible to it, including KPC producers; efficacy is shown mainly for complicated UTI.
Polymyxin B or colistin is reserved for severe laboratory-confirmed carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infection such as A. baumannii, usually as part of combination therapy.
Polymyxins are reserved for severe carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa infection; polymyxin B is usually preferred over colistin except for urinary tract infection.
In adult sepsis from a skin or soft-tissue source, vancomycin is added to the empiric regimen when MRSA is suspected.

text: Among first-choice options for hospital-acquired pneumonia, only piperacillin-tazobactam covers P. aeruginosa; prefer it with recent antibiotic exposure or known Pseudomonas colonisation.
Mild community-acquired pyelonephritis, mostly caused by E. coli, can be treated with oral ciprofloxacin.
Severe pyelonephritis, mostly caused by E. coli, is treated with cefotaxime or ceftriaxone and/or amikacin or gentamicin, combined in very sick patients.
Amikacin or gentamicin should be considered for pyelonephritis where ESBL-producing isolates are highly prevalent, as carbapenem-sparing options.
Cloxacillin, or another IV antistaphylococcal penicillin, is the first choice for acute bacterial osteomyelitis, where S. aureus is the main pathogen.
Clindamycin is acceptable for osteomyelitis caused by community-acquired MRSA if the isolate is susceptible or local MRSA keeps high clindamycin susceptibility.
If MRSA is resistant to clindamycin, or community-acquired MRSA is highly prevalent, vancomycin can be considered for osteomyelitis when S. aureus is suspected.
For catheter-related bloodstream infection with methicillin-resistant S. aureus, vancomycin or teicoplanin is preferred, with catheter removal.
Daptomycin is the alternative for MRSA catheter-related bloodstream infection.
For methicillin-susceptible S. aureus bloodstream infection, cefazolin or cloxacillin is preferred; vancomycin is less effective and kept for beta-lactam intolerance.
For carbapenem-resistant E. coli catheter-related bloodstream infection, colistin is the preferred agent.
